passages.text: In 1917 the French composer Erik Satie proposed a kind of music that nobody was supposed to listen to. He called it musique d'ameublement, or furniture music. He imagined it occupying a room the way wallpaper or an armchair does: present, useful, but never demanding attention. At a gallery in Paris in 1920, Satie and his colleague Darius Milhaud had a small ensemble play short, repetitive pieces during the intermission of a play. According to a well-known account, the audience promptly fell silent and returned to their seats to listen, and Satie hurried among them urging them to keep talking and walking about. By its own peculiar standard, the experiment was a failure. Yet the notion proved prophetic. Within a few decades, recorded background music was being piped into elevators, offices, and shops, engineered precisely so that people would not notice it. In 1978 the British musician Brian Eno released an album intended for airports. He wrote that such music should be as ignorable as it is interesting. Satie's whimsical provocation, it turned out, had anticipated an entire way of hearing.

In a short essay written in 1769, the French philosopher Denis Diderot described a curious misfortune. A friend had given him a splendid scarlet dressing gown, and he discarded his old one, shabby but comfortable. Soon the new garment made everything around it look drab. His straw chair seemed unworthy of it, so he replaced it with a leather armchair. Then the desk, the bookshelves, and the tapestries had to be upgraded in turn, until his modest study had become an elegant room, and he felt, as he put it, less master of his gown than its slave. Two centuries later, the anthropologist Grant McCracken gave the phenomenon a name: the Diderot effect. A single new acquisition can disrupt the apparent harmony among our possessions. It can set off a chain of further purchases, each one justified by the last. Retailers understand this well, which is why a new phone is sold beside cases, chargers, and headphones designed to match it. The implication is not that we should never buy anything new, but that the true cost of a purchase may include everything it persuades us to buy next.

Writers and students speak of deadlines so casually that the word's grim history is easily forgotten. During the American Civil War, the Confederate prison at Andersonville, Georgia, held tens of thousands of Union soldiers in a crowded and filthy stockade. A short distance inside the outer wall ran a marked line. Guards had orders to shoot any prisoner who crossed it. The prisoners called it the dead line. After the war, the term surfaced at the trial of the camp's commander, Henry Wirz, convicted and hanged in 1865. In the early twentieth century, the word drifted into the vocabulary of printing. There it seems to have referred to a guideline on a press beyond which type would not print. Newspaper offices then gave it the meaning familiar today: the time by which a story must be submitted. By the 1920s journalists were using deadline in this sense, and the expression soon spread to other trades and to ordinary speech. The modern deadline still carries a faint echo of menace, though missing one now costs a reprimand rather than a life.

The European eel is a fish whose life cycle posed, for centuries, one of natural history's most stubborn riddles. Fishermen caught adult eels in rivers all over Europe, yet no one had ever found an eel egg or a newborn eel. Aristotle concluded that eels arose spontaneously from mud. The answer began to emerge in the early twentieth century, when the Danish biologist Johannes Schmidt spent years trawling the Atlantic for the tiny, transparent, leaf-shaped larvae of eels. He noticed that the farther west he sailed, the smaller the larvae became, and he traced the smallest of all to the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic thousands of kilometers from European shores. The eels, it seemed, swim there to spawn and die. Their offspring drift back toward Europe on ocean currents, a voyage that may take years. Remarkably, nobody has yet observed European eels spawning in the wild, and scientists still debate how the adults navigate such an immense distance. The question has acquired urgency, because the number of young eels reaching European coasts has fallen precipitously since the 1980s.

In the 1980s the psychologist James Pennebaker asked a group of college students to write for fifteen minutes on four consecutive days. Some wrote about the most upsetting experiences of their lives, while others described neutral subjects such as their rooms or their shoes. ①<u>Many of those who wrote about trauma found the exercise painful, and some left the sessions in tears.</u> Yet in the months that followed, they visited the campus health center less often than students in the comparison group. ②<u>Later studies have linked such expressive writing to modest improvements in mood and sleep, although not every experiment has replicated the effect.</u> ③<u>Many universities now require students to submit their essays electronically rather than on paper.</u> Why should putting distress into words help at all? ④<u>Pennebaker came to believe that the benefit lies less in venting emotion than in organizing it, turning a chaotic memory into a coherent story.</u> Participants whose essays showed an increasing use of words such as because and realize tended to improve the most, as if understanding had gradually replaced mere turmoil.

Timbuktu, on the southern edge of the Sahara in what is now Mali, was a renowned center of learning in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Scholars there transcribed and composed manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine, and poetry, and families preserved these works for generations, often hidden in wooden chests or buried in the sand to protect them from invaders and damp. When armed militants seized the city in 2012, librarians and families dreaded that the collections would be destroyed. In a clandestine operation, they packed many thousands of manuscripts into metal trunks and smuggled them south to the capital, Bamako, by road and by river, often passing through hostile checkpoints. When the militants fled in early 2013, they set fire to a library building, but most of the manuscripts had already been spirited away. The rescue preserved an archive that refutes an entrenched prejudice, namely that Africa south of the Sahara possessed no written intellectual tradition. The more formidable challenge today is conservation. The fragile pages suffer in the humid climate of Bamako, and efforts are under way to digitize them.

On August 8, 2024, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck off the coast of Kyushu in southern Japan, near the edge of a vast undersea fault known as the Nankai Trough.
[A] The response revealed how difficult it is to convey an uncertain risk. Some vacationers canceled trips to beaches along the Pacific coast, and stores reported runs on bottled water and emergency supplies, even though officials stressed that they were not predicting a disaster.
[B] For the first time, the Japan Meteorological Agency responded by issuing a special advisory. It warned that the chance of a far larger earthquake along the trough, which has unleashed devastating quakes and tsunamis in the past, had risen slightly above its usual level.
[C] When the advisory was lifted a week later without incident, critics complained that it had harmed tourism for nothing. Seismologists replied that this was the wrong lesson: a slightly elevated risk of catastrophe is still worth knowing about, and the absence of a quake did not mean the warning had been mistaken.

Hildegard of Bingen was a twelfth-century abbess who defies categorization as thoroughly as any figure of the Middle Ages. Born in 1098 into a noble family in the Rhineland, she was entrusted to a religious community as a child. She eventually became the abbess of her own convent. From early childhood she experienced visions but kept them largely to herself until middle age, when she began to record them in a series of books that won the cautious approval of the pope. Yet visionary writing was only one of her pursuits. She composed dozens of liturgical songs, and their soaring melodies are still performed and recorded today. She also wrote a musical drama about the struggle between the virtues and the devil. She wrote treatises on medicine and natural history describing the healing properties of plants, stones, and animals. She corresponded with popes and emperors, occasionally rebuking them sharply. In her sixties she undertook preaching tours, an extraordinary activity for a woman of her era. In 2012, more than eight centuries after her death, the Catholic Church formally declared her a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

Nora's aunt ran an alteration shop in a single narrow room beneath a stairway in the old market, and for most of her childhood Nora regarded it as the most tedious place on earth. [A] When her mother began working evenings, Nora was sent there after school, and she spent the first weeks sulking among bolts of lining fabric and jars of mismatched buttons. Her aunt barely spoke to her. She worked with pins pressed between her lips, chalking lines on trousers and coats that customers had outgrown, outlived, or inherited. [B] One afternoon a man brought in a wool suit that had belonged to his late father and asked whether it could be made to fit him for his daughter's wedding. The aunt studied the jacket for a long time, turning it inside out and running her thumb along the seams. [C] "Your father was broader in the shoulders," she said at last, "but he stood the same way you do." She showed Nora how the original tailor had left generous seams, almost as if he had expected the suit to be altered someday. Then she let the girl unpick the stitches and explained what each one had been for. When the man returned two weeks later and tried on the jacket, he stood in front of the mirror for a long while without saying anything. [D] Then he thanked the aunt quietly and paid without looking at the bill. After he left, the aunt handed Nora a needle and a spool of gray thread. Nora did not realize until years later that her aunt had been waiting all along for her to show an interest.

For much of the twentieth century, psychologists who studied trauma concentrated, understandably, on the damage it inflicts: the nightmares, the hypervigilance, the sense of a future foreshortened. Yet clinicians persistently heard something else from survivors of bereavement, illness, and disaster. Alongside their suffering, many reported that the ordeal had changed them in ways they valued. They felt a deeper appreciation for ordinary days, a closer bond with the friends and relatives at their side, or a surprising confidence that they could endure whatever came next. In the mid-1990s the psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun gave this pattern a name, posttraumatic growth. They also devised a questionnaire to measure it. They were careful to underscore what the concept does not mean. Growth does not erase distress; the two often coexist for years. Nor is the trauma itself the source of any benefit. In their account, growth arises from the struggle to make sense of what has happened. Survivors are forced to rebuild beliefs about the world that the crisis has shattered. The notion has attracted criticism as well as enthusiasm. Some researchers suspect that reports of growth partly reflect wishful thinking. Such a comforting story may not match any measurable change in behavior. Others worry that popular accounts transform growth into an obligation, so that survivors who simply feel wounded come to believe they have failed. Tedeschi and Calhoun themselves cautioned that growth should never be demanded of any survivor.

When the program AlphaGo defeated the champion Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul in March 2016, many observers anticipated a bleak future for professional baduk. If a machine could defeat the best humans, what was the purpose of human competition? Lee himself retired in 2019, citing the dominance of artificial intelligence among his reasons. Yet the game has not declined; if anything, it has flourished. A study published in 2023 analyzed millions of moves made by professional players over several decades. It found that the quality of their decisions improved considerably after AlphaGo appeared, while their play also became more inventive, departing more often from conventional patterns. Players now train with AI programs that assess every position. A generation of young professionals has acquired insights overlooked by centuries of human play. The transformation is not universally endorsed. Some veterans lament that openings have grown homogeneous, as players imitate the engines rather than develop a personal style, and that memorizing machine-approved sequences can substitute for understanding. Still, the evidence thus far suggests that a superhuman opponent has made human players stronger rather than rendering them redundant.

Clara Wieck was born in Leipzig in 1819. Her father, a piano teacher of formidable and overbearing ambition, set out to make her a virtuoso. He succeeded spectacularly. By her teens she was performing across Europe to considerable acclaim. Before she turned seventeen, she had completed a piano concerto of her own. Her father was considerably less pleased when she fell in love with one of his former pupils, the composer Robert Schumann, and he fought the match so bitterly that the couple had to take him to court before they could marry in 1840. In the years that followed, Clara bore eight children, managed the household, and kept performing, often championing her husband's music before skeptical audiences. After Robert suffered a mental collapse and died in an asylum in 1856, she sustained the family largely through her concert tours. These continued for decades. She composed far less after her marriage and sometimes doubted that a woman should compose at all, yet her songs and piano works are now increasingly performed. Her portrait once appeared on the German hundred-mark banknote, a tangible measure of how her reputation has grown.

Ostriches do not, in fact, bury their heads in the sand when danger approaches; the image is an ancient misunderstanding. Yet economists borrowed it to name a very human habit. The ostrich effect is the inclination to evade information we suspect will be unpleasant. People show it even when the information would help them make better decisions. In one study, researchers examined how often investors in Sweden logged in to check their accounts. When markets were rising, they looked frequently, as if eager to savor good news. When markets were falling, the number of visits dropped noticeably. Comparable avoidance appears in medicine, where some people postpone screening tests for fear of a frightening result. It also appears in household finance, where unopened bills accumulate on the kitchen table. The behavior is easy to understand. Bad news stings, and ignorance offers a transient refuge from anxiety. But the refuge is illusory. The underlying facts do not change while we look away; the investment keeps losing value and the illness keeps progressing. Acknowledging the impulse is the first step toward resisting it, and some people find it easier to schedule regular, routine checks so that each look does not demand a fresh act of courage.

On a Sunday morning in October 2025, shortly after the Louvre opened its doors to visitors, a small group of thieves raised a lift mounted on a truck to an upper window of the Apollo Gallery, the gilded hall that houses the remnants of the French crown jewels. They cut through the window, smashed display cases, and escaped with several pieces of nineteenth-century jewelry within minutes. In their haste they dropped a crown of the empress Eugénie. It was later recovered, though damaged. The museum closed for the day, and an intensive manhunt commenced. The brazen theft provoked anguish and humiliation in France, but also a dispute that extended well beyond one museum. How could the most visited museum in the world have been so conspicuously vulnerable? Critics pointed to antiquated alarm systems and to audits whose warnings had gone unheeded. Museum directors elsewhere conceded an uncomfortable truth: institutions that exist to display treasures to millions of people can never be sealed like bank vaults, and every gain in openness carries some measure of risk. The theft thus exposed a dilemma that no alarm system can fully resolve.

The Tasmanian devil, a stocky, aggressive carnivorous marsupial about the size of a small dog, survives in the wild only on the Australian island of Tasmania. In 1996 a photographer noticed devils with grotesque swellings around their mouths and faces. The cause proved to be one of the most bizarre diseases known: a cancer that is itself contagious. Devils frequently bite one another on the face while feeding and mating. The bites transfer living tumor cells from one animal to another, and the cells grow there like a parasite. Infected devils usually perish within months, often of starvation once the disfiguring tumors make eating impossible. As the disease spread across the island, devil populations declined by roughly eighty percent. Authorities responded by establishing healthy insurance populations in zoos and on an offshore island. More recently there has been a faint glimmer of hope. Genetic studies suggest devils in some heavily affected areas are evolving resistance. A few animals have even been observed recovering from their tumors. Whether evolution can outpace the disease remains a matter of conjecture.

Most people can say whether they are hungry or tired, but far fewer can tell, without touching their wrist, how fast their heart is beating. This sense of the body's internal state is called interoception. In a common laboratory test, volunteers silently count the beats of their heart over a short interval. Their tally is then compared with an electronic recording. ①<u>Some people are remarkably accurate, while others miss many beats or count beats that never occurred.</u> These differences appear to matter well beyond the laboratory, with implications for mental health. ②<u>The heart pumps blood through a network of vessels that, laid end to end, would stretch for many thousands of kilometers.</u> Several studies have found that people who perceive their heartbeats more accurately also report experiencing emotions more intensely. The finding echoes an old idea: feelings are partly the mind's reading of bodily changes. ③<u>The link may also run in a troubling direction, since a person who misreads ordinary sensations as danger may be prone to anxiety.</u> ④<u>Researchers are therefore testing whether interoception can be trained, for example by having people check their counts against a monitor.</u> The early results are promising, but the field remains young.

High on a limestone cliff in western Iran, beside an ancient road, the Persian king Darius I ordered an enormous inscription carved around 520 BCE to proclaim his victories over rebels. The text was repeated in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian, all written in wedge-shaped cuneiform. For more than two millennia virtually nobody could read it. In the 1830s and 1840s a British army officer, Henry Rawlinson, made copies of the inscription, at times balancing on ladders and ropes above a sheer drop. Because Old Persian used a relatively small set of signs and could be compared with known later languages, it was deciphered first, and it subsequently served as a key to the far more complex Babylonian script. Skeptics doubted the decipherment and suspected its claims were largely speculative. In 1857, a newly discovered Assyrian text was sent to four scholars, including Rawlinson, who translated it independently and in secret. When their sealed versions were opened and compared, they agreed closely. The learned world was convinced that cuneiform could indeed be read, and the libraries of ancient Mesopotamia opened to modern study.

Time spent in nature is widely thought to benefit health, but how much of it a person needs has long been unclear. A study published in 2019 tried to answer that question using survey data from roughly twenty thousand adults in England. Participants reported how many minutes they had spent in parks, woodlands, beaches, and other natural settings during the previous week, as well as how they rated their own health and well-being. The researchers found a striking threshold. People who had spent at least 120 minutes in nature were substantially more likely to report good health and high well-being than those who had spent no time there at all. Those with less than 120 minutes showed no clear advantage. The benefit leveled off at around 200 to 300 minutes, so that longer stays yielded little additional gain. Intriguingly, it did not seem to matter whether the time was taken in one long excursion or in several short visits spread across the week. The study was correlational, so it could not prove that nature caused the improvement; healthier people may simply go outdoors more. Even so, a weekly target of two hours is a modest and attainable goal.

The buyer arrived on a gray morning in March, a younger man from a harbor two hours down the coast, and he walked twice around the boat that had belonged to Hana's father before saying anything at all.
[A] Hana had anticipated feeling relief. For three years after her father's death the boat had sat at the pier, costing the family considerable mooring fees, and every storm warning sent her down to the harbor in the dark to check the ropes. Her mother had stopped asking when she would sell it, and the silence was worse than the asking.
[B] Instead, as the man knelt to inspect the hull, Hana found herself listing things he had not asked about: the engine her father had rebuilt one winter in their kitchen, the dent near the bow from a night when the fog came in faster than anyone predicted, the radio that worked only if someone tapped it twice. The buyer listened courteously and nodded as if each blemish were a credential.
[C] When they had signed the papers, he asked whether she wanted to take the boat out one last time. She said no, and then she said yes. They went out past the breakwater together, and he let her steer. On the way back he did not talk, and she was grateful. At the pier she handed him the keys and the small notebook in which her father had recorded every repair for thirty years, and she walked home without looking back, something she had not known she could do.

During the pandemic, when travel abroad became virtually impossible and crowded indoor spaces felt risky, camping in Korea surged in popularity. [A] Campsites once tranquil on weekdays were booked weeks in advance. Outdoor retailers reported booming sales of tents and portable stoves, and television programs followed celebrities cooking over open fires. A particularly Korean variation, chabak, or sleeping in one's car, attracted people wanting the outdoors without the labor of pitching a tent. With the rear seats folded down and a mattress laid in the back, an ordinary sport utility vehicle could become a bedroom parked beside a beach or a lake. [B] The boom brought tribulations as well as pleasures. Residents of coastal villages complained that car campers occupied public parking lots for days, idled their engines through the night, and left behind heaps of refuse. [C] Several local governments responded by prohibiting overnight stays in particular parking areas or by designating official sites with toilets and waste collection. Safety officials, for their part, repeatedly warned campers against using fuel-burning heaters inside closed tents and vehicles, where carbon monoxide can accumulate without any warning smell. [D] As borders reopened, some expected that the craze would fade. It has cooled from its peak, but camping appears to have settled into a durable habit for many families. The implication for local authorities is that a pastime once deemed marginal now demands the same planning as any other form of tourism.

In the summer of 2025, a band called the Velvet Sundown attracted more than a million monthly listeners on a major streaming service before acknowledging that its songs had been created with the help of artificial intelligence. The episode brought into focus anxieties that had been accumulating for some time. Generative software can now produce a passable pop song in seconds, complete with lyrics and a synthetic voice. One streaming platform reported that a substantial share of the tracks uploaded to it each day were made entirely by machines. For listeners, the immediate issue is one of transparency. Many feel deceived when they discover that a singer they admired does not exist, and some services have begun labeling music generated by AI. For musicians, the stakes are economic. Streaming royalties are divided according to the number of plays, so an avalanche of cheap, automated tracks dilutes the income of human artists, many of whom already earn very little. Yet outright prohibition is neither feasible nor evidently desirable, since numerous artists now use AI tools for tasks such as mixing or composing backing parts. The most promising policies, critics suggest, concentrate on disclosure and on preventing fraudulent streams rather than on banning the technology.

Tawdry, meaning cheap and showy, has a surprisingly saintly origin. In the seventh century an Anglo-Saxon princess named Æthelthryth, later known as Saint Audrey, founded an abbey at Ely in eastern England. According to a story recorded by the historian Bede, she suffered in her final illness from a painful swelling on her neck. She regarded it as a just punishment for her youthful fondness for wearing necklaces. Centuries later, an annual fair held at Ely in her honor became renowned for selling silk neckbands known as Saint Audrey's lace. At first the lace was presumably a respectable souvenir, but over time the merchandise of the fair acquired a reputation for being garish and poorly made. Spoken quickly, Saint Audrey's lace was shortened to tawdry lace. By the late seventeenth century tawdry was being used on its own to describe anything cheap and vulgar in its decoration. The word thus preserves, fused from a saint's name, the memory of a medieval marketplace and of the gradual decline of its wares from emblems of devotion to objects of dubious quality.

After the First World War, the Australian government granted land in Western Australia to thousands of former soldiers, encouraging them to grow wheat. By 1932 the farmers confronted a peculiar adversary. Some twenty thousand emus, large flightless birds that migrate inland after their breeding season, had descended on the farmland, devouring crops and trampling fences. When the veterans appealed for help, the Minister of Defence dispatched a small detachment of soldiers armed with two machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition. The operation, launched in November, swiftly degenerated into a humiliation. The birds scattered into small groups whenever the soldiers approached, ran at astonishing speed, and proved surprisingly difficult to kill. On one occasion a gun jammed just as a large flock came within range. After several weeks and thousands of rounds, the military withdrew, having killed only a modest fraction of the birds. Newspapers mocked the campaign, and a politician asked in Parliament whether medals were to be struck for the birds. In later years farmers relied instead on a bounty system and on better fencing, which proved far more effective than soldiers had been.

For more than a century, railway lines have sliced through the hearts of Korean cities, carrying passengers and freight but also dividing neighborhoods, generating noise, and forcing pedestrians to detour around fences and level crossings. Relocating those tracks underground has long been an aspiration of urban planners, and one celebrated precedent shows what can be gained. When a section of the Gyeongui Line in western Seoul was moved below ground, the corridor it vacated was transformed into a long, narrow park lined with trees, coffee shops, and bookstores. The park quickly became one of the city's most popular places to stroll. In 2024 the National Assembly passed a special act intended to make such projects feasible on a far larger scale. The central idea is that the land freed by burying the tracks can be redeveloped and sold. The proceeds would then help finance the enormously expensive tunneling. Advocates envision rail corridors across the country reborn as green spaces and new districts. Skeptics question whether land values outside the capital are high enough to cover the costs. They warn that the projects could become a heavy fiscal burden if the anticipated development fails to materialize.

The bar-tailed godwit is a wading bird that probes mudflats for worms and shellfish, and it holds a remarkable record. In October 2022, a young godwit fitted with a tiny satellite tag took off from Alaska and did not touch down again for eleven days. When it finally landed in Tasmania, it had flown roughly 13,500 kilometers without a single stop. The distance is believed to be the longest nonstop flight ever recorded for a bird. Godwits cannot rest on the open ocean, so the journey demands extraordinary preparation. In the weeks before departure, the birds gorge themselves until fat accounts for more than half of their body weight. At the same time, organs they will not need in flight, such as parts of the digestive system, shrink dramatically, while the heart and flight muscles enlarge. The birds also appear to time their departures to coincide with favorable winds from passing storms. These winds can carry them a considerable part of the way. Scientists continue to investigate how they navigate with such precision across thousands of kilometers of featureless sea. What is already evident is that the bird's physiology is finely tuned to an undertaking that would be fatal to almost any other animal of its size.

When we are upset, we often try to push our feelings aside, yet simply putting them into words may do more good than we expect. The psychologist Matthew Lieberman and his colleagues showed volunteers photographs of angry or frightened faces while scanning their brains. ①<u>Some were asked to pick a word such as "angry" or "scared" to describe each face, while others were told to choose which of two first names suited it instead.</u> Those in the first group showed less activity in the amygdala, a brain region that reacts to threats. Lieberman calls this effect affect labeling. ②<u>The idea is that naming an emotion engages regions of the brain involved in language and reasoning, which seem to quiet the alarm that the feeling would otherwise set off.</u> ③<u>Because the technique requires only a single word, it can be used almost anywhere and costs nothing.</u> ④<u>Dictionaries of emotion words have become popular gifts at many bookstores, where they are displayed beside diaries every season.</u> The psychologist cautions that the technique is not a cure for serious mood disorders. As a way of steadying oneself during an argument or a tense moment, however, it appears to be surprisingly helpful.

For most of the twentieth century, the invention of abstract painting was credited to a handful of men, among them Wassily Kandinsky. He produced his first nonrepresentational canvases around 1910. Yet in 1906 a Swedish painter named Hilma af Klint had already begun a series of vast, vividly colored works composed of spirals, petals, and geometric forms that represented nothing in the visible world. She was a trained and respected artist who earned her living painting conventional landscapes and portraits. Her abstract works arose from an entirely different source. She belonged to a small circle of women who held séances, and she believed that spiritual guides had commissioned her monumental paintings. Doubting that her contemporaries would understand them, she rarely exhibited the works and stipulated that they should not be shown publicly until at least twenty years after her death. She died in 1944, and it was not until the 1980s that her abstractions reached a wider audience. In 2018 an exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York became the most visited show in that institution's history, prompting art historians to reconsider a narrative they had long deemed settled.

In 1933 the Chicago Symphony Orchestra gave the premiere of the Symphony in E minor by Florence Price, making her the first African American woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra.
[A] That precarious legacy was rescued by chance. In 2009 a couple preparing to renovate an abandoned house in St. Anne, Illinois, discovered boxes of her manuscripts, including two violin concertos and a symphony that had been presumed lost. The house had once been Price's summer home.
[B] The achievement was all the more remarkable given the formidable obstacles she had confronted. Born in Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1887, she had moved north to escape racial violence. She raised her children largely on her own after a difficult marriage and supported them by teaching and by writing popular songs under a pseudonym.
[C] Despite that early triumph, her reputation dwindled after her death in 1953. Orchestras rarely programmed her music, and much of it remained unpublished, scattered among private collections or simply unaccounted for.
Since the discovery, performances and recordings of her works have multiplied. Price is increasingly recognized not as a historical curiosity but as a composer of genuine distinction.

The dog appeared at the bus terminal during the first cold week of November, a lean yellow mongrel with one torn ear, and for several days nobody paid him much heed. Jisu was working the ticket window on the late shift that winter, selling seats on the last buses to the mountain villages. She noticed him because he always arrived around nine and lay down beside the radiator near Gate 4. Mrs. Bae, who ran the snack kiosk, was the first to feed him. She claimed she was only getting rid of day-old rice cakes. Then the cleaner, Mr. Seo, who complained loudly about the hair on his freshly mopped floor, quietly brought an old blanket and folded it beside the radiator. The drivers named him Gate Four. Within a month he had a water bowl, a collar donated by a passenger, and a small cardboard sign, written by a schoolgirl, asking people not to step on his tail. What none of the staff could explain was why he kept coming. One night, when a bus from the eastern villages pulled in late, Jisu watched him rise, walk to the door, and examine each passenger as they stepped down. Then he went back to his blanket. Mr. Seo mentioned that a farmer from that route had died in the autumn, and that the farmer had always taken his dog to town. After that, nobody at the terminal complained about the hair. They understood at last whom the dog came to meet every night, and that the terminal, without quite deciding to, had become a place for him to keep doing it.

For generations the public library was defined by silence: long rows of shelves, reading tables, and a librarian ready to hush anyone who spoke above a whisper. In recent years, however, libraries in many countries have been remodeled into something closer to community centers. [A] Helsinki's central library, Oodi, which opened in 2018, devotes most of its floor space not to books but to sewing machines, 3D printers, recording studios, and kitchens that visitors can reserve. Many Korean cities have followed a similar course, renovating aging libraries with coffee shops, children's play areas, and terraces, and some report that visitor numbers have risen sharply after reopening. The rationale is partly practical. [B] As more reading and research move online, libraries must justify their budgets with services that a screen cannot provide. It is also civic. A library is one of the few indoor public spaces where anyone may stay for hours without buying anything. Planners increasingly see it as a remedy for loneliness and a meeting ground for people of different ages and backgrounds. [C] Not everyone is pleased. Students preparing for examinations and older readers complain that the new libraries are noisy and that quiet study spaces have shrunk to make room for events. [D] Some librarians fear that the emphasis on attractive spaces has diverted funds from collections and professional staff. The most successful renovations seem to be those that separate the lively and the contemplative, designating clearly zoned quiet floors so that a library can serve as a bustling public square without ceasing to be a refuge.

The plan to replace the old covered market with a parking garage drew <u>vociferous</u> opposition from residents, who packed the council chamber and shouted down every speaker in favor of it.
arboreal
sporadic
covert
clamorous
vociferous 는 '시끄럽게 외치는, 목소리 높이는'이라 clamorous 와 가까워요. 회의장을 메우고 찬성 발언을 고함으로 막았다는 뒤 내용이 단서예요. arboreal(나무에 사는)은 문장과 관계없고, sporadic(산발적인)·covert(은밀한)는 소리 높여 반대하는 모습과 맞지 않아요.

Choose the one that is closest in meaning to the underlined word.
Rather than confront the director, several actors <u>surreptitiously</u> rewrote their own lines during rehearsals, hoping that nobody would notice the changes before opening night.
covertly
reluctantly
flagrantly
vehemently
surreptitiously 는 '남몰래, 슬그머니'라 covertly 와 같은 뜻이에요. 감독과 맞서지 않고 아무도 모르기를 바랐다는 내용이 단서예요. flagrantly(노골적으로)는 반대이고, reluctantly(마지못해)·vehemently(격렬하게)는 숨긴다는 뜻이 없어요.

The museum's founder was famously <u>parsimonious</u>, reusing old envelopes and refusing to heat the galleries in winter even as he spent a fortune acquiring paintings.
lavish
irascible
gregarious
stingy
parsimonious 는 '몹시 인색한'이라 stingy 와 가까워요. 봉투를 다시 쓰고 난방도 안 했다는 예가 단서예요. lavish(아낌없는)는 반대이고, irascible(성마른)·gregarious(사교적인)는 돈 쓰는 태도와 관계없어요.

Many travelers are convinced that searching for flights late at night guarantees a cheaper fare. Analyses of millions of ticket prices, however, suggest that such savings are largely ____: airlines adjust fares according to demand, route, and the date of departure, not the hour at which a customer happens to click.
exorbitant
illusory
perpetual
tangible
however 뒤에서 항공사는 수요·노선·날짜로 값을 정할 뿐 검색 시각과는 관계없다고 하니, 밤에 찾으면 싸다는 이득은 '착각에 불과한(illusory)' 거예요. tangible(실제로 손에 잡히는)은 반대이고, exorbitant(터무니없이 비싼)·perpetual(영원한)은 문맥과 맞지 않아요.

After three weeks of high fever, the patient sank into a profound ____. She slept through most of the day and showed little interest in food, visitors, or even the letters her grandchildren sent. Her doctors assured the family that such exhaustion was common during a long convalescence and would lift as her strength returned.

Researchers long wondered ②<u>how such a shape could form</u> inside a soft, round intestine. A team that examined wombats ③<u>killed in road accidents</u> found that the final section of the gut has walls of uneven stiffness, which ④<u>squeeze</u> the waste into cubes. The animals then stack the droppings on rocks and logs, probably to mark their territory.

a peculiarity 라는 선행사가 있으므로 관계대명사는 that 이나 which 여야 해요. what 은 선행사를 품은 관계대명사라 앞에 명사를 둘 수 없어요. how such a shape could form 은 간접의문문 어순(how+주어+동사), killed 는 수동 분사, squeeze 는 복수 walls 와 맞아요.

For more than a century, Thomas Edison was believed ①<u>to have made</u> the first recording of a human voice in 1877. That honor now ②<u>is belonging</u> to Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, a Parisian printer whose device could write sound waves onto paper ③<u>but could not</u> play them back. In 2008 American researchers converted into sound a set of his tracings ④<u>made in 1860</u>, revealing the faint voice of someone singing a French folk song.

belong 은 '~에 속하다'라는 상태를 나타내는 동사라 진행형으로 쓰지 않아요. is belonging 이 아니라 belongs 가 맞아요. to have made 는 believed 보다 앞선 일을 나타내는 완료부정사, but could not 은 could write 와 짝을 이루는 대등 구조, made in 1860 은 tracings 를 꾸미는 과거분사예요.

Choose the expression that best completes the passage.
When Melvil Dewey published his classification scheme in 1876, many libraries shelved books by size or by the date on which they had been acquired. Dewey divided knowledge into ten main classes, each assigned a block of a hundred numbers. Every class could be subdivided by adding digits after a decimal point. Critics have since pointed out its biases, such as the meager range of numbers it originally allotted to religions other than Christianity. Even so, the beauty of the system was that ____: a new book on, say, beekeeping could slip into place beside its neighbors without forcing librarians to renumber the rest of the collection.
it could expand indefinitely without disturbing existing numbers
it obliged libraries to purchase new shelves every single year
it treated the physical size of a book as its defining feature
it arranged every book strictly by the year of its first publication
콜론 뒤에서 새 책이 다른 책 번호를 바꾸지 않고 제자리에 들어간다고 했어요. 소수점 뒤로 숫자를 붙여 '기존 번호를 건드리지 않고 끝없이 늘릴 수 있다'는 것이 장점이에요. 크기나 날짜로 꽂던 방식은 듀이 이전의 모습이에요.

Choose the expression that best completes the passage.
Sailors in the age of sail had no speedometer. Yet they needed to know how fast their ships were moving in order to estimate their position. Their solution was ingeniously simple. A wooden board weighted to float upright was tossed overboard, trailing a line in which knots had been tied at regular intervals. Speed at sea is still measured in knots today, long after satellites have made the old wooden log obsolete. The reason lies in how the measurement was taken: while one sailor watched a small sandglass, another counted ____.
how many knots slipped away while the ship lay at anchor
how many waves struck the hull before the glass was empty
how many knots slipped through his fingers before the sand ran out
how many sailors climbed up the rigging while the sand was still falling
모래시계가 다 떨어질 때까지 손가락 사이로 풀려 나간 매듭 수를 세면 곧 속도가 되고, 그래서 지금도 바다 속도 단위가 knot 라고 이어져요. 파도·선원 수는 매듭과도 속도와도 관계가 없고, 닻을 내리고 서 있는 배로는 속도를 잴 수 없어요.

Choose the expression that best completes the passage.
On the morning of All Saints' Day in 1755, an earthquake, followed by a tsunami and days of fire, devastated Lisbon, then one of the wealthiest cities in Europe. The catastrophe shook more than buildings. Voltaire attacked the fashionable optimism of his age, first in a poem on the disaster and later, more famously, in his satirical novel Candide, whose cheerful tutor insists that all is for the best even as calamity follows calamity. What he found grotesque, in the face of so much innocent suffering, was the claim of several influential thinkers that ours was the best of all possible worlds, ____.
so that even apparent evils must serve some greater good
and that earthquakes could be foretold by careful study
and that such suffering showed how badly the world was made
although few of them had ever traveled beyond their homeland
볼테르가 무고한 희생 앞에서 이 생각을 끔찍하게 여겼고, 캉디드의 가정교사가 재앙 속에서도 '모든 것이 최선'이라 우긴다고 했어요. 그러니 빈칸은 '겉보기 악도 더 큰 선에 쓰인다'는 낙관론이 맞아요. 지진 예측은 그 철학과 관계없고, 세상이 잘못 만들어졌다는 것은 낙관론과 정반대예요.

Choose the expression that best completes the passage.
In 1865 the English economist William Stanley Jevons published The Coal Question, a book that economists still invoke when they ask whether more efficient cars, lights, or computers will genuinely reduce the total consumption of energy. Its central puzzle troubled many of his contemporaries. James Watt's improvements had made steam engines far more efficient, so that each engine burned much less coal to perform the same work. One might expect such efficiency to conserve the nation's coal, but Jevons argued the opposite: by making steam power cheaper, efficiency encouraged so many new uses that Britain ____.
returned to water power
exported its engines abroad
stopped mining coal altogether
consumed more coal than ever
효율이 좋아져 증기 동력이 싸지자 새 쓰임이 너무 많이 생겼다는 흐름이니, 영국은 '어느 때보다 많은 석탄을 썼다'가 맞아요. 같은 문장 앞쪽의 '석탄을 아낄 것 같다'와 반대(but … the opposite)라는 말이 단서예요. 채굴 중단·수력 회귀는 근거가 없어요.

quell

forecast
